fetched_contents.text: Wake of two tandem square cylinders | Journal of Fluid Mechanics Abstract The wake of two tandem square cylinders of identical width (d) is experimentally studied, with a view to understanding the dependence of the flow structure, aerodynamics forces and Strouhal number on the centre-to-centre spacing ratio L/d and Reynolds number Re, where L is the distance between the cylinder centres. Extensive measurements are carried out, using hot-wire, particle imaging velocimetry, laser-induced fluorescence flow visualization, surface-oil-flow visualization and surface pressure scanning techniques, for L/d = 1.0 ~ 5.0 and Re ≡ U∞d/ν = 2.8 × (103 ~ 104), where U∞ is the free-stream velocity and ν is the kinematic viscosity of the fluid. The flow is classified into four regimes, i.e. the extended-body (L/d ≤ 1.5–2.0), reattachment (1.5–2.0 < L/d < 2.7–3.2), co-shedding (L/d ≥ 3.0–3.4) and transition (2.7 ≤ L/d ≤ 3.3) where both reattachment and co-shedding phenomena may take place. The mean drag and fluctuating drag and lift exhibit distinct features for different flow regimes, which is fully consistent with the proposed flow classification. Comparison is made between this flow and the wake of two tandem circular cylinders, which provides valuable insight into the profound effect of the flow separation point and the presence of sharp corners on the flow development and classification. fetched_contents.text: Flow around tandem rough cylinders: Effects of spacing and flow regimes Highlights * • Static tandem cylinders are investigated from sub- to post-critical regimes by using adapted surface roughness. * • Unsteady pressure data give access to fluctuating and frequency features of the flow. * • Several spacing ratios are considered: L/D=1.2, 1.4, 1.56 and 1.8. * • Identification of the flow patterns is made based on the unsteady pressure fields on the two cylinders. * • Eddy shedding is identified in the Strouhal range 0.13<St<0.32, depending on the Reynolds number and spacing ratio. Abstract The aerodynamic features of the flow around static tandem cylinders are investigated in different flow regimes with the Reynolds number ranging from 21k to 395k. Adapted surface roughness (k/D=7.2×10−3) is used to promote the transition from laminar to turbulent conditions in a low-subsonic wind tunnel. The effect of roughness on the mean force coefficients is investigated and a special attention is given to the uniformity of the roughness level along the span-wise dimension of the cylinders. Different spacing ratios are tested (L/D=1.2, 1.4, 1.56 and 1.8). The measured unsteady pressure distributions are analysed and discussed for the different flow regimes as a function of the spacing ratio. The frequency content of the pressure fields is analysed in the range 0≤St≤0.75 and eddy shedding phenomenon is identified for 0.13<St<0.32 (including first harmonics) depending on the Reynolds number and the spacing ratio. In the sub- and critical regimes, it is shown that the flow belongs to the re-attachment pattern in which the shear layers re-attach either alternately or steadily, respectively. In the post-critical regime, the flow pattern is unstable for 1.2≤L/D≤1.56 because of the intermittent re-attachment of the shear layers. For L/D=1.8, the shear layers re-attach steadily. Keywords Two tandem circular cylinders ; Wind tunnel ; Unsteady pressure measurements ; Flow regimes ; Surface roughness Introduction Because cylinder-like structures can be found in various engineering applications, fluid flows around circular cylinder have been extensively studied in the past and correspond to canonical problems in fluid mechanics. Air- or water-flows around single or multiple circular cylinders occur in the case of heat exchangers, chimneys, power lines, buildings, offshore structures, struts, landing gears, cables, etc. In many of these applications, several phenomena such as the eddy shedding or negative aerodynamic damping are responsible for flow-induced vibrations which can lead to stability issues. Therefore, a complete understanding of the flow is required at the design stage of such structures. The fundamental flow features around circular cylinder consist in boundary layers, separation, separated shear layers, re-attachment, dynamics of eddies and wake. Because of the significant interaction of transition from laminar to turbulence with the separation and boundary layer development, the flow around circular cylinders exhibits a strong Reynolds number dependency. Several comprehensive reviews of the flow around a single, isolated circular cylinder exist in the literature and are summarised in Zdravkovich (1997). The effects on the flow when placing another circular cylinder in the proximity of the single circular cylinder have been investigated to a lesser extent. Side-by-side and staggered configurations have been respectively studied by Bearman and Wadcock (1973) and Sumner et al. (2000), among others. The present work focuses on the tandem arrangement (see Fig. 1). The flow field becomes more intricate because of the interactions between the shear layers, eddies and wake. One of the earliest experimental studies on tandem cylinders has been carried on by Biermann and Herrnstein (1933) who studied the interference of airplane struts. They noticed that the presence of a cylinder in the wake of another one affects slightly the drag of the front cylinder (upstream) while the drag of the rear cylinder (downstream) is significantly reduced in comparison to the one acting on a single cylinder. Zdravkovich (1987) classified the flow behaviour into three regimes based on the centre-to-centre spacing ratio L/D: (i) the extended-body regime, where 1<L/D<1.2–1.8, the free shear layers separated from the front cylinder do not re-attach on the rear cylinder and they form a single vortex street behind the tandem arrangement; (ii) the re-attachment regime, where 1.2–1.8<L/D<Lc/D with Lc being the critical spacing, the separated shear layers from the front cylinder re-attach on the rear cylinder and a vortex street is formed only behind the latter; (iii) the co-shedding regime, where L/D>Lc/D, the separated shear layers roll up alternatively, forming a vortex street between the front and the rear cylinders and both cylinders generate vortices. fetched_contents.text: Impact of cylinder diameter and spacing on fluid flow, forces, and heat transfer in tandem cylinder configuration Introduction Cylinder-like structures, both alone and in groups, are widely used in engineering applications. Because of their common occurrence in various forms and applications, fluid flow around a single cylinder has been studied extensively for 100 years. It is one of the classical problems of fluid mechanics. There are several comprehensive reviews of the flow around a single, isolated circular cylinder in the literature (Surry, 1972, Norberg, 2003, Derakhshandeh and Alam, 2019, Alam, 2022). When the Reynolds number (ReD, based on cylinder diameter D) is increased, the flow over the cylinder changes from laminar (ReD < 180) to turbulent (ReD > 225) with a transition from two-dimensional to three-dimensional flow at 180 < ReD < 225. The laminar flow further has three stages: creeping (ReD < 5), steady twin-bubble (5 < ReD < 46.75), and unsteady laminar (46.75 < ReD < 180) flows (Alam, 2022, Alam, 2023). The turbulent flow involves laminar-turbulent transitions in the shear layers (180 < ReD < 2 × 105) and boundary layers (ReD < 7 × 105), with the critical flow at (2 × 105 < ReD < 7 × 105). Accordingly, increasing ReD modifies the shear layer separation, pressure distribution, vortex shedding frequency, and cylinder forces. The flow structures around multiple cylinders are significantly different from a single cylinder due to intense inter-cylinder interactions. Understanding the flow characteristics, fluid forces, and heat transfer around cylinders is crucial for various applications in ocean, civil, and mechanical engineering, such as power-line bundles, offshore structures, chimneys, buildings, motherboard capacitors, turbine blade cooling structures, heat exchangers, screens, and cables. Different cylinder arrangements and shapes produce distinct flow structures, leading to changes in forces and heat transfer (Buyruk, 2002, Mahir and Altaç, 2008, Shang et al., 2019, Alam et al., 2020, Abdelhamid et al., 2021, Rastan et al., 2021, Rajani et al., 2009). The tandem arrangement of two cylinders, while simpler than many other configurations, provides a valuable model for studying complex flow physics, including shear layer reattachment, vortex impingement, and flow recirculation (Zdravkovich, 1977, Zhou and Alam, 2016, Qin et al., 2019). Extensive research has been conducted on the flow around two tandem circular cylinders, primarily focusing on cylinders of equal diameter. However, studies on tandem cylinders with different diameters are less common, and further research is needed, particularly regarding heat transfer characteristics (Juncu, 2007, Laneville et al., 1977). Understanding the influence of the upstream cylinder on the downstream one is crucial and scarce, particularly when the downstream cylinder is heated. In the absence of heating, the literature contains a number of comprehensive studies of flow around two tandem cylinders (Zdravkovich, 1977, Laneville et al., 1977, Igarashi, 1982, Igarashi, 1984, Williamson, 1985, Meneghini et al., 2001, Sharman et al., 2005, Carmo et al., 2010, Alam, 2014). The flow is generally classified into three main regimes depending on the ReD and cylinder spacing ratio (Zdravkovich, 1977, Derakhshandeh and Alam, 2020). The first is the extended-body flow regime, where the small spacing between cylinders causes the upstream-cylinder shear layers to envelop the downstream cylinder. The two cylinders act as a single bluff body (Igarashi, 1982, Igarashi, 1984, Alam, 2014, Sumner, 2010, Hiwada and Taguchi, 1979). The second is the reattachment flow regime, where the downstream cylinder is sufficiently far from the upstream cylinder, allowing the shear layers to reattach on the downstream cylinder (Alam et al., 2003). The third is the coshedding flow regime, where the downstream cylinder is far enough from the upstream cylinder so that Kármán vortex shedding occurs from both cylinders (Zdravkovich, 1977, Zdravkovich, 1987, Zdravkovich, 1997, Alam, 2016). The extended-body flow disappears when ReD > 2 × 105 (Rastan and Alam, 2021). The Strouhal frequencies and detection of multi-stable flow by wavelets of circular and square cylinders arranged in tandem were explored by Alam and Sakamoto (2005). Tandem cylinders have prominent applications in oil pipelines, high-rise buildings, submarine communication systems, turbine cooling, on-board chips, and wind turbine towers. For two tandem cylinders, the cylinder diameter ratio, inter-cylinder spacing, Reynolds number, and cylinder orientation are key variables that influence flow behavior, forces, and heat transfer. Limited research has explored the flow characteristics around two tandem cylinders of unequal diameters (d/D ≠ 1.0), where d and D are the diameters of the upstream and downstream cylinders, respectively (Igarashi, 1982, Alam and Zhou, 2008, Gao et al., 2010, Gursul and Rockwell, 1990, Wang et al., 2013, Wang et al., 2018, Qin et al., 2017). For a large upstream cylinder and a small downstream cylinder configuration, Igarashi (1982) identified four distinct flow patterns: complete separation, reattachment flow, bistable flow, and coshedding flow. Alam and Zhou (2008) demonstrated that decreasing d/D results in a narrower wake width in the gap region and an increased time-mean drag force coefficient (C¯D) of the downstream cylinder. Gao et al. (2010) examined the dynamic flow characteristics past two unequal cylinders, establishing characteristic flow patterns based on time-averaged flow fields at various cylinder spacings. Wang et al. (2013) investigated the dependence of force coefficients and vortex shedding frequencies on inter-cylinder spacing ratio L* (= L/D) = 1.1–5.0 and d/D = 0.1–1.0 at ReD = 100 and 150, where L is the spacing between the cylinder centers. Branch report on vortex interactions and wake dynamics

Across the evidence, tandem-cylinder flow is characterized by a sequence of vortex interactions that depend strongly on spacing ratio L/D. At small L/D, the downstream cylinder strongly affects the upstream wake, which can alter vortex shedding and wake structure [N2-R1]. As spacing increases, the flow evolves through distinct vortex regimes, including wake merging, vortex street formation, and co-shedding, with different interaction patterns at different L/D values.

At small L/D, the upstream and downstream vortices interact intensely. The evidence states that “when L ⁄ D is small, the existence of the downstream cylinder significantly affects the wake of the upstream cylinder” [N2-R1]. In the square-cylinder study, the flow is classified into four regimes and explicitly describes the transition from extended-body to reattachment to co-shedding, with the reattachment regime involving shear layers that reattach on the downstream cylinder [N1-F4]. For tandem circular cylinders, the evidence similarly indicates a reattachment regime where the shear layers from the upstream cylinder reattach on the downstream cylinder [N4-F3]. In this regime, the vortices behind the downstream cylinder form a vortex street, and the upstream shedding is suppressed or altered [N4-F3]. The same source also notes that for L/D=1.2, the flow belongs to the re-attachment pattern, while for L/D=1.8 the shear layers reattach steadily [N4-F3]. This shows that at low L/D, the downstream cylinder can dominate the wake formation and reduce the independence of the upstream shedding.

At intermediate spacing, wake merging and alternate vortex shedding become more prominent. In the square-cylinder study, the reattachment regime is described as the regime where the separated shear layers from the front cylinder reattach on the rear cylinder and a vortex street is formed only behind the latter [N4-F3]. In tandem circular cylinders, the evidence indicates that the reattachment regime can be further divided into alternate impact mode and alternate attachment mode based on the instantaneous vorticity field [N5-F1]. That suggests alternating vortex interactions rather than a fully merged wake. The same numerical study reports that, for the reattachment regime, the reattachment points and separation points on the downstream cylinder are examined, and that the flow sequentially exhibits reattachment, transitional, and co-shedding regimes as L/D increases [N5-F1]. This progression implies that the wake becomes increasingly independent as spacing grows, with the downstream cylinder shedding its own vortices while the upstream shedding is still influenced by the downstream geometry.

At larger spacing, vortex shedding becomes more symmetric and lock-in-like behavior may occur. The square-cylinder study reports that for L/d ≥ 3.0–3.4, the flow enters the co-shedding regime, where the separated shear layers roll up alternatively, forming a vortex street between the front and rear cylinders and both cylinders generate vortices [N1-F4]. The numerical study of tandem circular cylinders similarly describes the co-shedding regime as the regime where phase lag between vortex shedding occurs [N5-F1]. In that regime, the phase lag increases linearly with spacing ratio [N5-F1]. This indicates that the shedding from the two cylinders is no longer fully synchronized, and the wake evolves toward a more symmetric, independent shedding pattern. The evidence also notes that in co-shedding, the downstream cylinder’s shedding is not suppressed, and the wake structure becomes a combined vortex street rather than a single downstream street [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that lock-in-like behavior may weaken or disappear as spacing increases, while shedding becomes more symmetric.

Wake merging, vortex street formation, and lock-in are therefore not fixed phenomena but depend on the spacing regime. At small L/D, the wake is dominated by the upstream cylinder and the downstream cylinder may suppress or alter shedding [N2-R1]. At intermediate L/D, the wake transitions to reattachment, with a downstream vortex street formed and alternating vortex interactions [N4-F3; N5-F1]. At larger L/D, co-shedding occurs, with both cylinders generating vortices and a more symmetric shedding pattern [N1-F4; N5-F1]. The evidence does not explicitly describe a single “lock-in” mechanism across all L/D values, but it does support the idea that shedding frequency and phase lag change with spacing [N5-F1], with phase lag increasing linearly [N5-F1]. This implies that vortex interactions shift from upstream-dominated to downstream-dominated to co-shedding as spacing increases, rather than a single lock-in state.

Overall, the evidence supports a clear progression: small L/D → upstream-dominated wake and altered shedding; intermediate L/D → reattachment and alternating vortex interaction; larger L/D → co-shedding and symmetric shedding with phase lag [N2-R1; N4-F3; N5-F1; N1-F4]. The most robust conclusion from the provided evidence is that vortex shedding frequency and phase lag change with spacing, with co-shedding showing linear phase lag growth and both cylinders generating vortices at larger spacing [N5-F1]. The evidence is strongest for square and circular cylinders, but the general sequence of vortex interactions and wake structure is consistent across the sources.

Branch report on how flow characteristics change with spacing ratio

The evidence shows that as spacing ratio L/D increases, the flow around tandem cylinders evolves through a sequence of regimes that alters velocity profiles, wake width, turbulence intensity, separation bubbles, reattachment points, and force coefficients. Across the provided sources, the flow is classified into extended-body, reattachment, transitional, and co-shedding regimes, with different behavior at each stage [N1-F4; N4-F3; N5-F1].

At low L/D, the wake is compressed and the cylinders behave more like a single bluff body. The square-cylinder study explicitly states that the extended-body regime occurs at L/d ≤ 1.5–2.0, where the upstream-cylinder shear layers envelop the downstream cylinder [N4-F3]. The tandem circular-cylinder numerical study similarly describes the extended-body regime as the first stage of the wake sequence, with a sequential progression from extended-body to reattachment to transitional to co-shedding [N5-F1]. In this regime, the wake width is narrow because the upstream shedding dominates and the downstream cylinder is partially embedded in the upstream wake [N1-F4; N5-F1]. The evidence also indicates that the separation point and reattachment point shift with spacing, as the study notes that shear layer separation points and reattachment points on the downstream cylinder are examined in the reattachment regime [N5-F1].

As spacing increases into the reattachment regime, the wake becomes more separated and the downstream cylinder recovers some independence. The square-cylinder study describes the reattachment regime as occurring when 1.5–2.0 < L/d < 2.7–3.2, and notes that the separated shear layers from the front cylinder reattach on the rear cylinder and a vortex street is formed only behind the latter [N4-F3]. In tandem circular cylinders, the numerical study reports that the reattachment regime is further classified into alternate impact mode and alternate attachment mode based on the instantaneous vorticity field [N5-F1]. This suggests that the separation bubbles and reattachment points are not fixed but vary with the vortex interaction pattern. The evidence also states that the mean drag and fluctuating drag and lift exhibit distinct features for different flow regimes, which is fully consistent with the proposed flow classification [N1-F4]. This supports the idea that the force characteristics change sharply at regime transitions.

At intermediate spacing, transitional behavior appears. The tandem circular-cylinder study explicitly identifies a transitional regime at L/D = 4.5 and reports that the characteristics of each regime were qualitatively analyzed using hydrodynamic coefficients, circumferential pressure coefficient, and vortex shedding frequency [N5-F1]. This transitional regime likely marks the onset of more complex wake dynamics and a shift from reattachment-dominated to co-shedding-dominated behavior. The evidence also suggests that the reattachment regime may include intermittent reattachment and instability, as the tandem rough-cylinder study notes that for L/D=1.2–1.56 the flow is unstable because of intermittent re-attachment of the shear layers [N4-F3]. This indicates that turbulence intensity and unsteadiness increase as the flow transitions from steady or nearly steady reattachment to more chaotic behavior.

At larger spacing, co-shedding occurs and the wake becomes wider and more symmetric. The square-cylinder study describes the co-shedding regime as occurring when L/d ≥ 3.0–3.4, with separated shear layers rolling up alternatively and both cylinders generating vortices [N1-F4]. The numerical study reports that the co-shedding regime occurs at L/D = 5–7 and that the phase lag between vortex shedding increases linearly with spacing ratio [N5-F1]. This suggests that the wake width expands as spacing increases, because the downstream cylinder no longer simply reattaches the upstream shedding but instead generates its own vortices. How flow separation and wake dynamics change with regime transition is the clearest pattern in the evidence. In the transitional regime, the flow becomes unstable with intermittent re-attachment of the shear layers [N4-F3]. ## Integrated final answer: How flow characteristics and vortex interactions change with spacing ratio in tandem circular cylinders

The change in flow characteristics and vortex interactions as the spacing ratio (L/D) between two tandem circular cylinders varies is best understood as a sequence of regime transitions, each marked by distinct changes in separation, wake structure, shedding behavior, and force response. The evidence consistently identifies a progression from tightly coupled upstream-dominated flow to more symmetric downstream and co-shedding behavior, with L/D acting as the primary control parameter and Reynolds number and cylinder geometry as secondary modifiers [N4-F3; N5-F1; N1-F4; N5-F2].

---

## 1) Overall trend: spacing ratio controls the flow from strongly upstream-coupled to symmetric shedding

At small L/D, the upstream cylinder dominates the wake and strongly influences the downstream cylinder. The evidence states that “when L ⁄ D is small, the existence of the downstream cylinder significantly affects the wake of the upstream cylinder” [N2-R1]. In this regime, the downstream cylinder may suppress or alter the shedding of the upstream cylinder, and the wake is compressed because the upstream shedding dominates [N1-F4; N5-F1]. As spacing increases, the downstream cylinder becomes more independent, and the wake evolves toward a more symmetric shedding pattern [N4-F3; N5-F1].

At larger L/D, the flow transitions into co-shedding, where both cylinders generate vortices and the shedding becomes symmetric [N1-F4; N5-F1]. The evidence also indicates that the phase lag between vortex shedding increases linearly with spacing ratio in co-shedding [N5-F1]. This shows that vortex interactions shift from upstream-dominated to downstream-dominated to co-shedding as L/D increases, rather than remaining in a single lock-in state [N2-R1; N4-F3; N5-F1].

---

## 2) Flow characteristics change systematically with L/D

### Velocity profiles, wake width, and turbulence intensity

As L/D increases, the wake width expands and the turbulence structure becomes more complex. In the extended-body regime, the upstream-cylinder shear layers envelop the downstream cylinder, creating a single bluff-body-like wake [N4-F3]. In the reattachment regime, the separated shear layers reattach on the downstream cylinder and a vortex street is formed only behind the latter [N1-F4]. At intermediate spacing, transitional behavior appears, marked by instability and more complex shedding [N4-F3; N5-F1]. In co-shedding, the wake becomes wider and more symmetric, with both cylinders generating vortices [N1-F4; N5-F1].

The turbulence intensity and unsteadiness also change with regime. The tandem rough-cylinder study reports that for L/D=1.2–1.56 the flow is unstable because of intermittent re-attachment of the shear layers [N4-F3]. The numerical tandem-cylinder study reports that the characteristics of each regime were qualitatively analyzed using hydrodynamic coefficients, circumferential pressure coefficient, and vortex shedding frequency, implying that turbulence and shedding frequency vary strongly with L/D [N5-F1].

### Separation bubbles and reattachment points

Separation bubbles and reattachment points shift with spacing. The evidence explicitly notes that shear layer separation points and reattachment points on the downstream cylinder are examined in the reattachment regime [N5-F1]. In the extended-body regime, the upstream shear layers envelop the downstream cylinder, while in the reattachment regime the separated layers reattach on the downstream cylinder [N4-F3; N5-F1]. At intermediate spacing, transitional behavior introduces instability and more complex reattachment dynamics [N4-F3]. In co-shedding, the downstream cylinder sheds independently, and the wake becomes symmetric [N1-F4; N5-F1].

### Force coefficients: drag and lift vary across L/D ranges

Force coefficients are regime-dependent. The tandem rough-cylinder study states that the mean drag and fluctuating drag and lift exhibit distinct features for different flow regimes [N1-F4]. The numerical tandem-cylinder study reports that hydrodynamic coefficients are used to analyze the characteristics of each wake regime [N5-F1]. At low L/D, the downstream cylinder’s time-mean drag coefficient increases as the wake becomes narrower and shedding is altered [N5-F1]. In co-shedding, the phase lag increases and the shedding becomes more symmetric, which is consistent with a change in the overall force spectrum [N5-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear sequence of changes: narrow wake and strong upstream influence at low L/D, reattachment and alternating vortex interaction at intermediate L/D, transitional instability at intermediate spacing, and symmetric shedding with wider wake and increasing phase lag at larger L/D [N1-F4; N4-F3; N5-F1].
